extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in mathematics, physics, or engineering studying dynamical systems and applications (biology, circuits, mechanics)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and modeling of planar ordinary differential equation systems arising in biology (predator–prey) and circuit theory (Liénard / van der Pol / FitzHugh–Nagumo), including hypotheses that guarantee equilibria, sinks/sources, limit cycles, and Hopf bifurcations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predator–prey sign and boundedness hypotheses (A,B)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist A>0, B>0 such that M(x,y)<0 if x>A and N(x,y)<0 if y>B; M(0,0)>0 and N(0,0)>0. The intersections of the curves M^{-1}(0) and N^{-1}(0) are finite and transverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the structural assumptions on the growth-rate factors M(x,y), N(x,y) that model: large populations experience negative growth, very small populations increase, and nullclines intersect finitely and transversely (no degenerate intersections). Used as hypotheses for global dynamical conclusions about trajectories in the rectangle 0<x<A, 0<y<B.

rubrics_metrics.name: All solutions tend to an equilibrium inside 0<x<A,0<y<B
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the predator–prey hypotheses above (existence of A,B and sign conditions plus finite transverse intersections), every solution tends to an equilibrium in the region 0<x<A, 0<y<B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a global attractivity conclusion derived from the sign/compactness/nullcline intersection assumptions; useful as a criterion for long-term coexistence tending to equilibria rather than unbounded growth or chaotic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: No sources in predator–prey region
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same predator–prey hypotheses, there are no source equilibria in the positive quadrant (0<x,0<y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of the sign and nullcline transversality assumptions; eliminates unstable repelling equilibria in the ecological model region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of at least one sink
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the predator–prey hypotheses, there is at least one sink (asymptotically stable equilibrium) in the positive region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topological/index-type argument from the configuration of vector field guarantees at least one attractor (sink) under these assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of global sink under monotonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: If additionally ∂M/∂x < 0 and ∂N/∂y < 0, then there is a unique sink Z, and Z is the ω-limit set for all (x,y) with x>0,y>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity (negative self-derivative) of the growth-rate functions rules out multiple sinks; yields global convergence of all positive initial conditions to the unique stable equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual destruction — no long-term coexistence (exercise statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system modeling two mutually destructive species (qualitatively: each species increases the death rate of the other) should be written; under plausible hypotheses, two mutually destructive species cannot coexist in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise invites formalizing the model and proving extinction/coexistence impossibility using sign structure and Lyapunov or trapping-region arguments; the qualitative criterion is that sufficiently strong mutual negative interactions preclude persistent coexistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predator–prey hypotheses (9a–9f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model x' = M(x,y)x, y' = N(x,y)y with conditions: (a) predators decrease if too few prey: N(x,y)<0 if x<b for some b>0; (b) ∂N/∂x > 0 (prey increases predator growth); (c) M(0,0)>0 (small prey increase absent predators); (d) ∃A>0 with M(x,y)<0 if x>A (prey constrained at large x); (e) ∂M/∂y < 0 (more predators decreases prey growth); (f) M^{-1}(0) and N^{-1}(0) intersect transversely and finitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard biologically motivated sign and monotonicity assumptions on functional factors M,N used to deduce existence of stable equilibria or limit cycles in predator–prey systems; they formalize notions like prey-limited predator growth and predator-limited prey growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichotomy: stable equilibrium or ω-limit cycle under (9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists (u,v) with M(u,v)>0 and N(u,v)>0 (a region where both species grow), then under hypotheses (9a–9f) the system has either an asymptotically stable equilibrium or an ω-limit cycle. Moreover, if the number of limit cycles is finite and positive, one must have orbits spiraling toward it from both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This result gives a bifurcation-type dichotomy: either coexistence at a stable fixed point or sustained oscillations (limit cycle). The extra statement about spiraling limit cycles identifies their stability character when finitely many exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified predator–prey parameter-region criterion (exercise 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the specific system x' = x(1−x) − a x y/(x+c), y' = b y(1−y/x), determine parameter-region where a stable equilibrium with x,y ≠ 0 exists; if that equilibrium is unstable, prove existence of a stable limit cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise asks to delineate parameter values (in a,b,c) for interior equilibrium stability and to show an unstable interior equilibrium implies a stable periodic attractor (Hopf/limit-cycle phenomenon) for this biologically motivated rational functional response model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kirchhoff current and voltage laws as modelling constraints (KCL/KVL)
rubrics_metrics.description: KCL: iR = iL = −iC (sum of currents at nodes). KVL: vR + vL − vC = 0 (sum of potential differences around loop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the physical constraints that reduce the full R3×R3 state space to the physical subspace: they must be enforced when writing circuit ODEs; used to eliminate variables and reduce dimensionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistor characteristic and generalized Ohm's law
rubrics_metrics.description: A resistor imposes a functional relation vR = f(iR) (the graph of f is the resistor characteristic); for a linear resistor f(i)=k i (Ohm's law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling choice: f may be nonlinear (e.g., tunnel diode characteristic). The shape/location of f is dynamical: a 'passive' resistor has its graph in the origin and interiors of the first and third quadrants, which has dynamical consequences (dissipation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Device differential relations: inductor and capacitor
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductor: (diL/dt)/L = vL (Faraday's law). Capacitor: C (dvC/dt) = iC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these constitutive relations to convert circuit constraints into time-evolution ODEs for chosen state variables (e.g., iL and vC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model reduction to Liénard form
rubrics_metrics.description: Using KCL, KVL and device relations and eliminating redundant variables, the RLC series circuit reduces (with L=C=1 and state x=iL, y=vC) to the Liénard system: x' = y − f(x), y' = −x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This canonical reduction illustrates how circuit laws produce planar systems of Liénard type; serves as template for analyzing oscillation/dissipation via Liapunov functions, nullclines, and Poincaré maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear characteristic: sink for k>0 and spiral condition
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x)=k x with k>0, linearization yields eigenvalues λ± = (−k ± sqrt(k^2 − 4))/2; the origin is a sink for any k>0 and a spiral sink if k<2; all solutions tend to the origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple criterion for global asymptotic stability in the linear resistor case (dissipative circuit). The eigenvalue formula gives precise conditions for oscillatory (spiral) versus nodal decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium classification via f'(0) for Liénard system
rubrics_metrics.description: The unique equilibrium of the Liénard system is at (0,f(0)); linearization matrix has eigenvalues λ± = (−f'(0) ± sqrt(f'(0)^2 − 4))/2, so the equilibrium is a sink if f'(0) > 0 and a source if f'(0) < 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local stability of equilibrium determined by slope of resistor characteristic at the operating point; used to predict whether the trivial equilibrium attracts or repels nearby trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyapunov function W and sign condition for global attractivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Define W(x,y) = 1/2 (x^2 + y^2). Then W' = − x f(x). If f(x)>0 for x>0, f(x)<0 for x<0, and f(0)=0, then W is a strict Lyapunov function on R^2 and all solutions tend to the unique equilibrium at the origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a direct, checkable criterion (sign of f matched to sign of x) for global asymptotic stability. In circuit terms this corresponds to a 'passive' resistor and the dissipative nature of the circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive resistor => global dissipation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A resistor is passive if its characteristic lies in the origin and the interiors of the first and third quadrants; then −x f(x) < 0 for x ≠ 0 and all solutions tend to the origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical interpretation: passivity of the resistor implies circuit 'deadness' (decay to zero), so check characteristic geometry to infer global damping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van der Pol special-case criterion: unique attracting limit cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: For f(x)=x^3 − x (the van der Pol case), the origin is a source, and there exists one nontrivial periodic solution; every other nontrivial solution tends to this periodic solution (the system oscillates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a canonical example where nonlinear negative damping near the origin and positive damping away create a unique stable limit cycle (relaxation oscillator behavior). The proof employs nullcline geometry, monotone Poincaré maps and an energy-type integral δ(y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré / semi-Poincaré map method for limit cycle uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a Poincaré return map P on half-line ν+; via construction of a semi-Poincaré map α and the function δ(y) = (α(y)^2 − y^2)/2, show δ(y) has one zero (positive then decreasing to −∞) which yields a unique fixed point of P and thus a unique periodic orbit attracting all other nonzero solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical criterion/method: analyze monotonicity and asymptotics of δ to show existence and uniqueness of periodic orbit and global attraction; provides a constructive method via return maps rather than abstract existence theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopf bifurcation criterion in parameterized Liénard family
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider f_µ(x) = x^3 − µ x. The linearization at the origin has eigenvalues λ± = (µ ± sqrt(µ^2 − 4))/2, so the origin is a spiral sink for µ<0 and a spiral source for µ>0. As µ increases through 0 a unique periodic solution γ_µ is born (Hopf bifurcation): γ_µ attracts all nonzero solutions for µ>0 and γ_µ → 0 as µ→0+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: sign crossing of linearization parameter µ through zero indicates a Hopf bifurcation; check linear stability change and then apply nonlinear Liénard analysis to get birth and stability of limit cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: FitzHugh–Nagumo parameter constraints and dynamical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: FitzHugh–Nagumo system x' = y + x − x^3/3 + I, y' = −x + a − b y with parameters satisfying 0 < (3/2)(1−a) < b < 1. For I=0 there is a unique equilibrium (x0,y0) which is always a sink; for I≠0 there remains a unique equilibrium (x_I,y_I) with x_I varying monotonically with I; for parameter values where the equilibrium becomes a source, there must exist a stable limit cycle. The system models excitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit parameter-range and qualitative-dynamical statements for the two-dimensional reduction of Hodgkin–Huxley: they provide criteria for existence/uniqueness/stability of equilibria and for the onset of oscillatory behavior (excitability and limit cycles). Exercises ask to locate bifurcations and sketch phase portraits in parameter planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy/integral computation method for sign properties (δ integral)
rubrics_metrics.description: For van der Pol analysis, define W and δ as integrals of −x(x^3 − x) (equivalently x^2(1−x^2)) along solution arcs; positivity on 0<x<1 implies δ>0 for small y, while negative large-x contributions force δ→−∞, giving sign change and uniqueness of periodic orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete criterion/method: express change in energy W along a trajectory as an integral whose integrand sign can be analyzed region-by-region to infer existence/uniqueness/stability of closed orbits.
